patient.name: Musa Kamara
patient.complaint: 13-month-old with 2 days of vomiting, watery diarrhoea and fever
background: Moved to Croydon from Sierra Leone at 9 months; missed rotavirus vaccine
Goes to nursery; several children off sick
Brought in by his mother, Aminata

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely causative organism?': outbreak in a closed setting (norovirus), a febrile child under 5 (rotavirus), or a milder subacute illness with conjunctivitis (adenovirus). Grading dehydration and shock is the key clinical decision.

points: Musa, 13 months: vomiting and **watery diarrhoea** for 2 days.
Fever of 38.9°C at home; no blood in the stool.
Fewer wet nappies today; sleepy and grizzly.
Missed his rotavirus vaccine; nursery outbreak.

steps.lead: Musa has an acute viral GI infection. It should settle in **1 to 3 days**; the danger is **dehydration**.
Musa is in the **rotavirus** peak (6 to 24 months), unvaccinated, and catching it from nursery.

steps.q: Which virus is most likely in Musa?
steps.r: Under 5, high fever, vomiting and watery diarrhoea, unvaccinated: **rotavirus**. Norovirus drives outbreaks in adults and closed settings.

steps.lead: Musa's high fever fits rotavirus; norovirus gives profuse vomiting **12 to 48 hours** after exposure; adenovirus is milder, with URTI or conjunctivitis.

steps.title: Which virus?
head: Virus
Who and where
Picture
rows: Any age; cruise ships, care homes, hospitals
Profuse vomiting, watery diarrhoea, **12–48 h** after exposure, lasts 1–3 days
Watery diarrhoea, **high fever**, vomiting; may need admission
Milder, subacute diarrhoea, low fever, URTI or conjunctivitis

points: Sunken eyes, dry mouth, no tears.
Cool hands and feet; **capillary refill 3.5 seconds**.

visual.title: Capillary refill time
visual.label: Musa 3.5 s
visual.caption: Refill over **2 to 3 seconds** with tachycardia and cold peripheries suggests clinical **shock**.

steps.lead: Musa's prolonged capillary refill, tachycardia and drowsiness mean he has moved from dehydration into **shock**.

steps.text: Do not label every vomiting child 'gastro'. **Bloody** stool, a bulging fontanelle, bilious vomiting or a rigid abdomen need another explanation.

investigation.exam: Expect a question where the answer is **no investigation**: viral gastroenteritis is clinical. Tests (stool sample, U&Es) are for severe, immunocompromised or persistent cases.

steps.q: Musa is shocked. Is investigation justified?
steps.r: Most children need nothing, but Musa is **severe**: check U&Es and send a stool sample.

steps.lead: Musa is severe, so he gets **U&Es** for dehydration and a **stool sample**.

steps.title: Musa's bloods
steps.text: Raised urea and creatinine from dehydration; low bicarbonate from stool losses and poor perfusion.

visual.title: Musa's urea
visual.label: Musa 9.4
visual.caption: A raised urea confirms what the bedside showed: **significant dehydration**.

steps.lead: Most of Musa's nursery classmates needed no tests at all: viral gastroenteritis is a **clinical diagnosis**.

steps.text: Stool PCR would find rotavirus, but in a well child it changes nothing. Test only when severe, immunocompromised or persistent.
Do not send a stool sample on every child with diarrhoea. The exam answer for a well, hydrated child is **no investigation**.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': ORS for mild to moderate dehydration, a **20 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus** for shock, and soap-and-water infection control in outbreaks.

steps.q: Musa is shocked. What is the first fluid step?
steps.r: Shock needs an **IV 20 mL/kg bolus** of isotonic crystalloid, then reassessment.

steps.lead: Musa weighs 10 kg, so he gets a **200 mL** bolus of 0.9% saline and is reassessed.

steps.title: Fluids by severity
nodes: Assess: capillary refill, pulse, BP, alertness
No dehydration: keep drinking, continue feeds
Mild to moderate: ORS little and often
Reassess, repeat if still shocked, then rehydrate

visual.title: Musa after the bolus
visual.caption: Pulse and refill improve after the bolus; he then moves on to oral rehydration.

steps.lead: Once Musa is out of shock he drinks **ORS**, the first-line treatment for mild to moderate dehydration; antiemetics help some patients keep fluids down.
On the ward Musa is nursed in a side room with **hand hygiene** to stop spread to other children.
Musa's fluids follow NICE diarrhoea and vomiting in children; his siblings should get the rotavirus vaccine on schedule.

steps.text: Antibiotics and antidiarrhoeal drugs have **no role** in viral gastroenteritis in children.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why alcohol gel fails for norovirus, how rotavirus causes diarrhoea, why rehydration and not antimicrobials is treatment, what vaccination changed.

steps.lead: Rotavirus destroyed Musa's mature **enterocytes** at the villous tips, so he lost absorptive surface and lactase.

steps.title: How rotavirus causes diarrhoea
nodes: Infects mature enterocytes at villous tips
Undigested sugars stay in the lumen

steps.lead: Musa lost fluid because his gut could not absorb it, not because the virus invaded: **rehydration** fixes that.

steps.q: Why did the ward use soap and water, not alcohol gel?
steps.r: **Non-enveloped** viruses such as norovirus resist alcohol; soap and water physically remove them.

steps.lead: If the ward had a **norovirus** outbreak, alcohol gel would not stop it; hand washing and isolation would.
Had Musa received the **rotavirus vaccine** in the UK schedule, his risk of hospital admission would have been much lower.

steps.text: After rotavirus, damaged brush border can leave **temporary lactose intolerance**: diarrhoea worse after milk for a few weeks.

mcq.q: Most common cause of gastroenteritis outbreaks on cruise ships?
Most common cause in children under 5?
When do norovirus symptoms start after exposure?

mcq.r: Milder, subacute; may come with conjunctivitis.

mcq.q: What capillary refill time suggests clinical shock?
What test is needed for a well child with 1 day of diarrhoea?
First-line treatment for mild to moderate dehydration?
What bolus is given for shock?
Why is alcohol gel poor against norovirus?

mcq.r: Loss of absorptive surface and lactase.

prompts.q: What is viral gastroenteritis, how long does it last and what is the main risk?

points.p: Acute viral GI infection causing diarrhoea and vomiting
Lasts 1–3 days
Dehydration is the main risk

prompts.q: Which virus causes which pattern, and who gets it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: setting and age decide the virus.

points.p: Norovirus: outbreaks in closed settings (cruise ships, care homes, hospitals)
Rotavirus: under 5s, peak 6–24 months, high fever
Adenovirus 40 and 41: milder subacute illness, URTI or conjunctivitis

prompts.q: How does norovirus present and when after exposure?

points.p: Profuse vomiting and acute watery diarrhoea
12–48 hours after exposure
Lasts 1–3 days

prompts.q: How do you recognise dehydration progressing to shock?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: capillary refill plus perfusion.

points.p: Capillary refill time over 2–3 seconds
Tachycardia, hypotension, cold or mottled peripheries
Drowsy or reduced consciousness, reduced urine output

prompts.q: When does viral gastroenteritis need investigation, and with what?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: usually the answer is none.

points.p: Mostly a clinical diagnosis; no investigation
If severe, immunocompromised or persistent: stool sample
U&Es to assess dehydration

prompts.q: How is dehydration treated by severity?

points.p: Mild to moderate: oral rehydration solution first-line
Antiemetics for symptom control
Shock: hospital, IV fluids, 20 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% saline

prompts.q: How do you stop it spreading?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: soap and water, not gel.

points.p: Hand hygiene with soap and water
Isolation of hospital cases
Rotavirus vaccine in UK childhood schedule

prompts.q: Why does rotavirus cause diarrhoea, and why is rehydration the mainstay?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: absorption fails, mucosa is not invaded.

points.p: Infects and destroys mature enterocytes at villous tips
Less disaccharidase activity: osmotic, lactose-intolerance-type diarrhoea
Fluid loss is secretory/osmotic, not mucosal invasion, so rehydrate

prompts.q: Why is alcohol gel less effective for norovirus, and what did rotavirus vaccination change?

points.p: Norovirus is a non-enveloped RNA virus resistant to alcohol
Rotavirus vaccine substantially reduced hospital admissions in children

glossary.gastroenteritis: Infection and inflammation of the stomach and intestines causing vomiting and diarrhoea.
glossary.norovirus: Non-enveloped RNA virus; the commonest cause of gastroenteritis outbreaks in closed settings.
glossary.rotavirus: Virus causing severe gastroenteritis in under 5s; prevented by a UK routine vaccine.
glossary.adenovirus: Virus family; serotypes 40 and 41 cause mild childhood gastroenteritis.
glossary.serotypes: Strains of a microbe distinguished by their surface antigens.
glossary.dehydration: Loss of body water faster than it is replaced.
glossary.shock: Inadequate tissue perfusion: prolonged capillary refill, tachycardia, cold peripheries, low BP.
glossary.capillary refill time: Seconds for skin colour to return after pressing; over 2 to 3 seconds suggests shock.
glossary.ORS: Oral rehydration solution: glucose and salts that drive water absorption.
glossary.oral rehydration solution: Glucose-electrolyte drink used first-line for mild to moderate dehydration.
glossary.antiemetics: Drugs that reduce vomiting, such as ondansetron.
glossary.bolus: A set volume of fluid given quickly through a drip.
glossary.isotonic crystalloid: Salt solution with the same concentration as plasma, such as 0.9% saline.
glossary.0.9% saline: Isotonic sodium chloride solution used for fluid boluses.
glossary.non-enveloped: A virus without an outer lipid layer, so it resists alcohol.
glossary.enveloped: A virus with an outer lipid membrane that alcohol can dissolve.
glossary.RNA virus: Virus whose genetic material is RNA, such as norovirus and rotavirus.
glossary.enterocytes: Absorptive cells lining the small intestine.
glossary.villous tips: Ends of the villi, where mature absorptive enterocytes sit.
glossary.disaccharidase: Brush border enzyme splitting sugars such as lactose.
glossary.lactase: Enzyme splitting lactose; lost temporarily after rotavirus.
glossary.lactose intolerance: Diarrhoea and bloating after milk due to lack of lactase.
glossary.osmotic diarrhoea: Watery diarrhoea caused by unabsorbed solutes pulling water into the gut.
glossary.secretory diarrhoea: Watery diarrhoea from active secretion of fluid by the gut lining.
glossary.outbreak: More cases than expected in one place over a short time.
glossary.closed settings: Places where people live close together, such as cruise ships, care homes and hospitals.
glossary.U&Es: Urea and electrolytes: blood tests of kidney function and salts.
glossary.PCR: Polymerase chain reaction: detects viral genetic material in a sample.
glossary.immunocompromised: Weakened immune system, for example after transplant or chemotherapy.
glossary.hand hygiene: Hand washing to stop spread; soap and water for norovirus.
glossary.isolation: Nursing an infectious patient apart from others to prevent spread.
glossary.rotavirus vaccine: Oral vaccine in the UK infant schedule preventing severe rotavirus.
glossary.mottled: Blotchy, patchy skin from poor circulation.
glossary.tacrolimus: Calcineurin inhibitor immunosuppressant used after transplant.

technique.stem: A 68 year old woman on a cruise ship has had profuse vomiting and watery diarrhoea for 12 hours. Thirty other passengers became unwell over the past 2 days with the same symptoms. Most recovered within 2 days. She has no blood in her stool.
technique.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?

steps.x: Organism question: the setting is the biggest clue.
Outbreak in a closed setting, vomiting-dominant, short and self-limiting.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Norovirus**.

elim: Point-source food poisoning within hours, not spreading over days.

steps.x: **C. Norovirus.** Rule: closed setting outbreak = norovirus.

technique.stem: A 4 year old girl has had vomiting and watery diarrhoea for 24 hours. Her brother had the same illness last week. She is drinking and passing urine. Her pulse rate is 110 bpm, capillary refill 1 second and she is alert and playful.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

steps.x: Is any test needed? Grade severity first.

clues: Her brother had the same illness
steps.x: Short illness, sick contact, well hydrated.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Viral gastroenteritis is a **clinical diagnosis**.

elim: Only if severe, immunocompromised or persistent.

steps.x: **C. No investigation.** Rule: well child = no tests.

technique.stem: A 2 year old boy has had diarrhoea and vomiting for 2 days. He has dry mucous membranes and is irritable. His pulse rate is 150 bpm, capillary refill 2 seconds and BP 92/58 mmHg. He keeps down small sips of fluid.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

steps.x: Initial management: grade dehydration first.
Clinical dehydration without shock; tolerating oral fluid.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **ORS** little and often.

elim: Not used in children with gastroenteritis.

steps.x: **D. Oral rehydration solution.** Rule: dehydrated but not shocked = ORS.

technique.stem: A 9 month old boy has had watery diarrhoea and fever for 3 days. Stool PCR is positive for rotavirus. His stools are watery and acidic.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his diarrhoea?
o: Destruction of mature enterocytes at villous tips

steps.x: Mechanism: name the virus, then its target.
Acidic stool = unabsorbed sugars fermented: osmotic diarrhoea.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Rotavirus kills **mature villous-tip enterocytes**, reducing absorption and disaccharidase activity.
**A. Destruction of mature enterocytes at villous tips.** Rule: rotavirus = villous tip enterocytes lost = osmotic.

practice.stem: A 74 year old man in a care home has had sudden profuse vomiting and watery diarrhoea for 18 hours. Eight residents and three staff developed the same illness this week, each lasting 1 to 3 days. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Outbreaks of profuse vomiting and watery diarrhoea in closed settings, lasting 1–3 days and spreading to staff, are norovirus.

steps.x: Organism question in a closed setting.
Outbreak in residents and staff, short vomiting illness.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Norovirus**.

elim: Antibiotic-related diarrhoea, not vomiting outbreaks in staff.
One food source, not person-to-person over a week.

steps.x: **B. Norovirus.** Rule: care home outbreak including staff = norovirus.

practice.stem: An 11 month old girl has had high fever, vomiting and profuse watery diarrhoea for 2 days. She has not received any routine vaccinations. Several children at her nursery are unwell. Her temperature is 39.0°C and pulse rate 156 bpm. There is no blood in the stool.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Rotavirus is the commonest cause in under 5s (peak 6–24 months), with high fever; the vaccine prevents most severe cases.

steps.x: Organism in a febrile infant.
Peak age 6–24 months, unvaccinated, high fever, watery diarrhoea.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Rotavirus**.
**E. Rotavirus.** Rule: unvaccinated infant + high fever = rotavirus.

practice.stem: A 3 year old boy has had loose watery stools for 8 days with a low-grade fever and occasional vomiting. He also has a runny nose and red, watery eyes. He is drinking well. His temperature is 37.8°C.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Enteric adenovirus (40/41) causes milder, subacute diarrhoea with low-grade fever, sometimes with URTI or conjunctivitis.

steps.x: Organism: a milder, longer illness with extra features.
Subacute diarrhoea with URTI and conjunctivitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Adenovirus** (serotypes 40 and 41).
**A. Adenovirus.** Rule: subacute diarrhoea + conjunctivitis = adenovirus.

practice.stem: A 32 year old man has had vomiting and watery diarrhoea for 36 hours. His partner had the same illness 2 days ago and has recovered. There is no blood in his stool, no recent travel and no antibiotic use. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. His abdomen is soft.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Acute watery diarrhoea and vomiting spread between close contacts, settling in 1–3 days, is viral gastroenteritis; bloody stools would suggest bacteria.

steps.x: Diagnosis in acute diarrhoea and vomiting.

clues: His partner had the same illness
steps.x: Short-lived illness passed between close contacts, non-bloody, soft abdomen.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Viral gastroenteritis**.
**E. Viral gastroenteritis.** Rule: acute D&V + sick contact + non-bloody = viral gastroenteritis.

practice.stem: A 15 month old boy has had diarrhoea and vomiting for 3 days. He is drowsy, with cold hands and feet and sunken eyes. His pulse rate is 176 bpm, capillary refill time 4 seconds and BP 70/38 mmHg.
practice.q: Which best describes his clinical state?
practice.e: Prolonged capillary refill above 2–3 seconds with cold peripheries, drowsiness, tachycardia and hypotension is clinical shock needing an IV bolus.

steps.x: Grade the dehydration.
Drowsy, cold peripheries, tachycardia, CRT over 3 seconds, hypotension.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Clinical shock**.

elim: No rash, neck signs or bulging fontanelle; the history is gastroenteritis.

steps.x: **A. Clinical shock.** Rule: CRT >2–3 s + cold + drowsy + hypotension = shock.

practice.stem: A 14 month old girl had rotavirus gastroenteritis 2 weeks ago. She is now well and feeding, but her watery diarrhoea returns after each bottle of cow's milk formula. She has no blood in her stool and is gaining weight. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her ongoing diarrhoea?
practice.e: Rotavirus destroys mature enterocytes and their disaccharidases, leaving temporary lactose intolerance with osmotic diarrhoea after milk.

steps.x: Cause of persistent diarrhoea after a viral illness.
Rotavirus damaged villous-tip enterocytes, which carry lactase.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Secondary (transient) lactose intolerance** after rotavirus.

elim: Needs gluten exposure and weight loss.
Starts in early infancy, with eczema or blood in stool.
Undigested food in stools, unrelated to milk, no recent infection.

steps.x: **D. Secondary lactose intolerance.** Rule: diarrhoea with milk after rotavirus = lost lactase.

practice.stem: A 26 year old woman has had vomiting and diarrhoea for 2 days after a colleague was ill with the same. She is drinking well. Her temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. She is not immunocompromised.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: Stool sample for culture and PCR
practice.e: Viral gastroenteritis is a clinical diagnosis; tests are reserved for severe, immunocompromised or persistent cases.

steps.x: Is a test needed?
Mild, short, sick contact, well, immunocompetent.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **No investigation**: clinical diagnosis.

elim: Only if severe, immunocompromised or persistent.

steps.x: **C. No investigation.** Rule: mild viral gastroenteritis = no test.

practice.stem: A 45 year old man who had a kidney transplant 1 year ago, on tacrolimus, has had watery diarrhoea and vomiting for 10 days. His wife had norovirus 2 weeks ago and recovered in 2 days. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 108/68 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
practice.e: Immunocompromised patients and persistent cases need a stool sample and U&Es; norovirus can become chronic in transplant recipients.

steps.x: Investigation: does anything make this patient different?
Immunocompromised and persistent: infection can be prolonged; dehydration threatens the graft.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Stool sample and U&Es**.

elim: Correct for well, immunocompetent people only.

steps.x: **E. Stool sample and U&Es.** Rule: immunocompromised or persistent = stool sample + U&Es.

practice.stem: A 3 year old boy has had diarrhoea and vomiting for 1 day. He is thirsty with a dry mouth but alert. His pulse rate is 128 bpm, capillary refill time 2 seconds and BP 96/60 mmHg. He has kept down small drinks.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Oral rehydration solution is first-line for mild to moderate dehydration; IV boluses are for shock.

steps.x: Initial management: grade first.

clues: thirsty with a dry mouth but alert
steps.x: Mild to moderate dehydration, not shocked, tolerating fluids.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **ORS** little and often.

elim: Wrong fluid; NG ORS only if refusing.

steps.x: **D. Oral rehydration solution.** Rule: mild to moderate = ORS.

practice.stem: A 10 month old girl (8 kg) with rotavirus gastroenteritis is drowsy with mottled skin. Her pulse rate is 182 bpm, capillary refill time 5 seconds and BP 64/36 mmHg. IV access is obtained.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Severe dehydration with shock needs a 20 mL/kg IV bolus of isotonic crystalloid (0.9% saline): 160 mL for an 8 kg child.

steps.x: Initial management of shock: work out the dose.
Shock: 20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid; 20 x 8 = 160 mL.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV 0.9% saline 160 mL bolus** (20 mL/kg), then reassess.

elim: Hypotonic, and too slow for shock.
Not first-line and 50 mL/kg is too much.
Too slow and unsafe when drowsy.

steps.x: **B. IV 0.9% saline 160 mL bolus.** Rule: shock = 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline, then reassess.

practice.stem: On a hospital elderly care ward, four patients and two nurses develop sudden vomiting and watery diarrhoea over 24 hours. Norovirus is confirmed on stool PCR. One patient's pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg; all are drinking.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate measure to control the outbreak?
o: Alcohol hand gel on entering bays
Close the bay, isolate patients and wash hands with soap and water
Oral ciprofloxacin for all patients on the ward
practice.e: Norovirus resists alcohol gel; outbreaks are controlled with soap-and-water hand washing, isolation and closing affected bays.

steps.x: Infection control in an outbreak.
Hospital norovirus outbreak.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Isolation, bay closure and soap-and-water hand washing**.

elim: Norovirus is non-enveloped and resists alcohol.

steps.x: **B. Close the bay, isolate patients and wash hands with soap and water.** Rule: norovirus = soap and water + isolation.

practice.stem: A 70 year old woman on a cruise ship develops vomiting and diarrhoea during a norovirus outbreak. The ship's crew had been cleaning hands with alcohol-based sanitiser throughout.
practice.q: Which property of norovirus best explains why the sanitiser failed?
o: It is a non-enveloped RNA virus
practice.e: Norovirus is a non-enveloped RNA virus resistant to alcohol; soap-and-water washing and isolation control outbreaks.

steps.x: Mechanism: a property of the organism.
Alcohol works by dissolving lipid envelopes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Norovirus is a **non-enveloped RNA virus**, so alcohol cannot disrupt it.

elim: The opposite: enveloped viruses are killed by alcohol.
Spread is faeco-oral, vomit aerosols and surfaces.

steps.x: **D. It is a non-enveloped RNA virus.** Rule: non-enveloped = alcohol-resistant.
